extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, judges, and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether asserted patent claims are directed to patent-ineligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101 using the Alice two-step framework, with emphasis on image-processing/software claims. Applies to claim drafting, prosecution, and litigation analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory baseline for patent eligibility (§101 and implicit exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 101 defines patent-eligible subject matter as any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any improvement thereof; the Supreme Court has explained there are 'implicit' exceptions: laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this statutory baseline as the starting point for inquiry; the Alice/Mayo framework is applied to determine whether a claim falls within an implicit exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice step one — determine whether claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept
rubrics_metrics.description: At step one, 'determine whether the claims at issue are directed to one of those patent-ineligible concepts' (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on the 'focus' of the claim as written; consider the claim in light of the specification but do not import limitations from the specification into the claim language. Examples of ineligible focuses include abstract ideas such as data manipulation, mental processes, and longstanding human activities implemented on a computer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that merely organize, alter, or manipulate data are likely abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that organize, alter, or manipulate data, without more, are patent ineligible (collecting precedents: Broadband iTV; Intell. Ventures; Elec. Power Grp.; Digitech).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim primarily recites receiving, analyzing, storing, transforming, or displaying data—especially using generic computing components—and does not explain a technical way the improvement is achieved, treat it as directed to an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional/results-oriented claim language without details is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims framed entirely in functional, results-oriented terms (describing what is accomplished rather than how) are suspect and may be treated as abstract; the district court characterized the claims as 'functional and ends-oriented.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that merely recite high-level steps such as 'determining', 'acquiring', and 'adjusting' without describing how those steps are performed or what specific technical rules/operations accomplish them are vulnerable at step one and step two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must explain how the arrangement achieves a technological improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely using new data or parameters does not render a claim patent eligible unless the claims (not just the specification) 'explain how these arrangements actually result in the claimed improvement.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To survive §101, claims should recite specific rules, algorithms, or constrained steps showing how the claimed elements produce a technological improvement (cf. McRo: claims 'limited to rules with specific characteristics'). General statements of improved result are not enough.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not import specification details into claim language during the §101 focus
rubrics_metrics.description: While the claims are considered in light of the specification, courts 'avoid importing concepts from the specification into the claims' and the §101 inquiry must focus on the language of the asserted claims themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing patent eligibility, ensure the claim text itself embodies the claimed technical detail; relying solely on detailed disclosure in the specification (without claim language support) is improper to escape abstraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice step two — inventive concept (transforming claim into patent-eligible application)
rubrics_metrics.description: At step two, 'consider the elements of each claim both individually and 'as an ordered combination' to determine whether the additional elements 'transform the nature of the claim' into a patent-eligible application.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for an inventive concept beyond the abstract idea—e.g., non-generic computer implementation, concrete technical improvements, or specific rules/algorithms. Mere recitation of applying correction conditions or parameters without more will not qualify as an inventive concept (citing Broadband, BSG Tech).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of generic computers or using computers 'as a tool' does not supply an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that merely use generic computing components or 'merely use computers as a tool' to implement an abstract idea do not supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the only novel aspect is automating a human activity using a conventional computer, the claim will likely fail §101 unless it recites specific computer improvements or unconventional configurations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapting existing technology to new data environments is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely adapting existing technology (e.g., machine learning) to a new field or data environment does not create patent eligibility if the claims do not describe how the improvement is achieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that 'apply machine learning to a new field of use' without describing the technical innovation in the learning/processing steps are likely abstract (citing Recentive Analytics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative-claim treatment is acceptable when claims are substantially similar
rubrics_metrics.description: A court may treat a single claim as representative and dismiss all claims if the others are 'substantially similar and linked to the same abstract idea' (Content Extraction & Transmission).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claims differ only by trivial variations (e.g., different labels for the same data types or slight refinements of the same functional steps), a representative-claim analysis is permissible; however, materially different claims require separate consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of inventive concept can be resolved from intrinsic record; factual disputes necessary only when present
rubrics_metrics.description: The absence of an inventive concept does not necessarily entail subsidiary factual determinations; 'a patent itself may establish that the claims contain no inventive concept' (Berkheimer acknowledged).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim language and specification on their face show no inventive concept, §101 can be decided as a matter of law. If the patentee points to genuine factual disputes about what the specification or claim elements mean, Berkheimer may require further factfinding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recitation of parameters without explaining what they are or how to manipulate them is inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting 'parameters' or 'correction conditions' without describing what those parameters are or how they should be manipulated does not turn an abstract data-manipulation concept into a patent-eligible invention (citing Hawk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should define the nature of parameters, their computation, mappings, or algorithms for manipulation; vague references to parameters or properties leave claims vulnerable under §101.
